questions.q: What runs a block of code that might fail, and what runs only if that code throws a terminating error?
options: try wraps the risky code; catch runs only on a terminating error
catch wraps the risky code; try runs only on error
finally wraps the risky code; try runs only on error
There is no difference between try and catch
questions.explain: try contains the code that might fail; catch fires specifically when a terminating error is thrown inside it.

questions.q: What does the finally block do?
options: Runs every time, whether the try block succeeded or the catch block fired — the right place for cleanup that always must happen
Runs only when an error occurs
Runs only when no error occurs
Is optional syntax with no actual execution behavior
questions.explain: finally always executes regardless of outcome, making it the right place for cleanup like closing a connection or writing a completion log line.

questions.q: Why does -ErrorAction Stop matter for a try/catch block wrapping a cmdlet like Backup-DbaDatabase?
options: Most cmdlets produce non-terminating errors by default, which do NOT trigger catch — -ErrorAction Stop forces that command's errors to be terminating so catch actually fires
It makes the backup run faster
It is required syntax for any cmdlet to run at all
It has no real effect and is purely cosmetic
questions.explain: Without -ErrorAction Stop (or $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'), a failing cmdlet's non-terminating error lets execution fall through to the next line as if it succeeded, and catch never runs.

questions.q: What does setting $ErrorActionPreference = "Stop" at the top of a script accomplish?
options: Sets terminating-error behavior as the script-wide default, without needing -ErrorAction Stop on every individual command
Disables all error handling in the script
Only affects the very last line of the script
Automatically emails the DBA team on any failure
questions.explain: It's a script-wide default rather than a per-command setting, useful for unattended maintenance scripts where any failure should stop and get logged.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does error handling matter more in DBA maintenance scripts than in a typical script?
options: An unhandled error mid-maintenance-job can leave a database in a genuinely bad state (a broken backup, a half-completed index rebuild, a partially applied security change)
PowerShell scripts for DBAs cannot use try/catch at all
DBA scripts never actually throw errors
It doesn't matter more; all scripts have identical risk
questions.explain: The blast radius of an unhandled error in a DBA script is production data — very different from, say, an incomplete report.
